newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's de Silguy sees euro in pocket sooner.
newsitem.headline: EU's de Silguy sees euro in pocket sooner.

text.p: Europe's monetary affairs commissioner said on Thursday the European Union should bring forward the introduction of single currency notes and coins, raising the prospect of euros in the pocket within 4-1/2 years.
Speaking at a conference called to discuss the practical aspects of the single currency, Yves-Thibault de Silguy also said national currencies should be phased out earlier than currently planned.

His comments underlined the growing confidence in Brussels that the move towards a single currency is irreversible, despite worries in Germany and elsewhere about the difficulties of getting national economies in order.
The current scenario calls for the euro to be introduced in qualifying EU countries on January 1, 1999 -- but only as a unit used by banks and other financial institutions.

Coins and notes have been scheduled to be issued on January 1, 2002, with national currencies such as the mark, French franc and guilder remaining legal tender for another six months alongside the euro.

But de Silguy, reflecting the concern of consumer and retail groups that a Christmas-time introduction of a new currency would be chaotic, suggested the new money could be put into circulation as early as autumn 2001.
National currencies could then be phased out ahead of mid-2002, he said.
The suggested six-month period of dual circulation for the euro and national currencies has been criticised in some circles for being too long.

De Silguy said he envisioned "a few weeks at the most". He said there were no legal difficulties in making such a move because the EU's treaty only requires coins to be circulated "by" January 1, 2002.
Such talk horrified at least one business group likely to be the most effected by the introduction of the currency.

The European Vending Association said bringing the euro forward and dropping national currencies early would cause its members a headache. It asked for assistance from the EU to meet the additional burden.
In a statement the group said some 3.15 million vending machines would need to be changed to fit the euro coin, each one taking about an hour to change.
Three years will be needed once a final design for the coin is chosen to produce the software and hardware upgrades necessary, it said.

Retailers attending the conference also were likely to have been disappointed by the annoucement. Although they do not want the coins to be released slap bang in the middle of their busiest season, they would prefer a delay.
A number said putting the coins into circulation in February 2002, when shoppers take a post-Christmas break, would be the best time.
De Silguy, however, appeared to be reflecting a growing consensus among the single currency's decision-makers.
Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner of a new EU central bank, has also called for the euro to be introduced earlier.
